Our matrix-level Schanuel-lemma method proves rigidity: under a finite-resolution hypothesis, the nonzero layer and degree uniquely determine a topological CSS code's translation SET order at the stable translation-invariant Clifford level. For prime qudits the hypothesis is automatic, and a finite layer's translation kernel gives the exact minimal coarse graining to a toric-code stack. We realize admissible single-layer data. Beyond this regime, split and nonsplit extensions of 3D qubit toric codes yield eight models sharing all identical $E_σ^\ell$ layers with trivial translation action but having distinct size-dependent ground-state degeneracies, hence distinct translation SET phases. Thus inter-layer gluing carries SET data invisible to individual layers.
one_liner: A homological superselection-profile framework classifies translation-enriched topological order in CSS stabilizer code families.
why_it_matters: It sharpens how topological quantum code phases are compared, including finite-size degeneracy data invisible to simpler excitation-layer invariants.
detailed_summary: The paper defines a topological superselection profile for translation-invariant CSS codes using derived Hom and Ext modules of stabilizer-map cokernels. For regular Koszul models, it computes the excitation layers explicitly, finds single-layer structure, and relates finite-size logicals to Tor. It also shows that split and nonsplit extensions of 3D qubit toric codes can share identical layer data while differing in size-dependent ground-state degeneracy, so inter-layer gluing carries distinct translation SET information.
main_result: The main result is a rigidity and classification framework for translation SET order, plus examples where nonsplit extensions distinguish phases beyond individual excitation layers.
application_angle: The framework can guide classification and construction of topological quantum memories and LDPC-style hardware architectures with translation symmetry.

title: Coupled-Layer Codes: Beyond Quantum Product Constructions
abstract: Product codes are an important class of quantum error-correcting codes constructed from multiple input codes, which can give rise to asymptotically good quantum low-density parity check codes. In previous work, we showed how the product between two codes can be physically implemented by coupling layers of the first code using checks of the second code. In this work, we further unify product code constructions with coupled-layer constructions of phases of matter by introducing coupled-layer codes. The essential strategy is to condense general excitations created by Pauli operators among multiple decoupled layers of the first code. The condensation is specified by an excitation algebra, which encodes the excitations, along with an algebra-preserving map. This coupling between layers generalizes the notion of gauging in physics as well as the mapping cone in homological algebra, and can be used to produce non-CSS codes. As examples, we show how coupled-layer codes reproduce the X-cube and Chamon models. We further generalize the balanced product code by allowing a unitary transformation in addition to a group action by free permutation and describe its corresponding coupled-layer construction. In particular, we show how balancing by a ZX-duality can reproduce non-CSS codes such as the fermionic toric code and the 3-fermion Walker-Wang model in 3D.
one_liner: Coupled-layer codes generalize product-code constructions by condensing Pauli-created excitations across code layers.
why_it_matters: The construction links quantum LDPC coding, gauging, and phases of matter while producing non-CSS codes beyond standard product recipes.
detailed_summary: The work introduces coupled-layer codes, where multiple decoupled layers of a base code are coupled by condensing excitations specified by an excitation algebra and algebra-preserving map. This framework generalizes both gauging in many-body physics and mapping-cone constructions in homological algebra. It reproduces X-cube and Chamon models and extends balanced product codes by allowing unitary transformations such as ZX duality, yielding non-CSS examples including fermionic toric code and 3-fermion Walker-Wang models.
main_result: The paper demonstrates a general coupled-layer construction that recovers known fracton models and generates broader CSS and non-CSS quantum code families.
application_angle: It expands the design space for physically motivated quantum error-correcting codes that may map more naturally onto layered hardware or topological media.

title: Phase diagram of lasing under correlated pump from GPU-accelerated Truncated Wigner dynamics
abstract: Superradiant (SR) lasers store optical coherence in the atomic medium rather than the cavity field, but the incoherent drive that sustains inversion imposes a trade-off: local pumping yields coherent light at a rate that grows linearly with the atom number $N$, heating the medium through photon recoil, whereas fully collective pumping removes this scaling but limits the emission to partial coherence. We interpolate between these limits employing a spatially correlated pump on a chain of $N$ two-level atoms, with rates decaying with distance between atoms as a power law of exponent $α$. To study systems beyond the reach of exact solutions, we employ the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA), whose independent trajectories are ideally suited to GPU parallelism. Harnessing this, we perform a full scan of the steady-state observables for up to $10^4$ atoms at a computational cost that is practical. Our findings indicate that ultra-narrow emission persists for all $α$, while the coherence improves as the pump becomes shorter ranged, with $g^{(2)} \to 1$ surviving at least down to $α\approx 1$, indicating that fully coherent light thus does not require local pumping. The drive strength needed for lasing is reduced by a factor $N^{1-α}$ for $α< 1$, and by $\log N$ as $α\to 1$, parametrically suppressing recoil heating; notably, $α= 1$ matches the far-field envelope of dissipative couplings in free space. The correlation range of the pump thus acts as a knob trading drive intensity, and the heating it causes, against optical coherence.
one_liner: GPU-accelerated Truncated Wigner simulations map how pump-correlation range controls coherence and heating in superradiant lasers.
why_it_matters: It identifies pump correlations as a practical knob for preserving narrow linewidth while reducing recoil heating in large atomic laser systems.
detailed_summary: The paper studies a chain of up to 10000 two-level atoms in a superradiant laser with spatially correlated incoherent pumping whose rate decays as a power law. Using GPU-parallel Truncated Wigner dynamics, it scans steady-state observables across pump strength and correlation exponent. The results indicate ultra-narrow emission across all exponents, with near-coherent statistics surviving down to about alpha equals 1 and lasing thresholds reduced for long-range correlated pumping.
main_result: The study shows that coherent, ultra-narrow emission can persist without strictly local pumping while the required drive and associated recoil heating are parametrically reduced.
application_angle: This is relevant to optical clocks, precision metrology, and low-noise photonic sources where linewidth and heating are central constraints.

title: Eliminating photon transport in long-baseline optical interferometry using quantum memories
abstract: In this paper, we describe the fundamental operating mechanisms of optical interferometry using quantum memory and entanglement. We show how these remove the optical delay line bottleneck. Quantum memory is not without its own set of challenges, some of which include very small bandwidths as well as limitations in storage time. We examine the influence of timing artifacts on memory photon capture probability and interferometric complex visibility. We highlight keystone areas of technology that require further development and are essential to realizing these opportunities, as well as ongoing work to overcome these challenges.
one_liner: Quantum memories and entanglement are proposed to replace photon transport and delay lines in long-baseline optical interferometry.
why_it_matters: The approach targets a core scaling bottleneck for astronomical interferometers by moving phase comparison into stored quantum states.
detailed_summary: The paper describes optical interferometry architectures that use quantum memories and entanglement rather than transporting photons through long optical delay lines. It analyzes operating mechanisms for memory-assisted visibility measurement and studies how timing artifacts affect photon capture probability and interferometric complex visibility. The authors also identify technology gaps, including memory bandwidth and storage-time limits, that must be addressed for practical deployment.
main_result: The main result is a technical operating framework showing how quantum memories can remove the optical delay-line bottleneck in long-baseline interferometry.
application_angle: It points toward more scalable astronomical and precision-sensing interferometers, provided quantum memory bandwidth, timing, and storage constraints improve.

title: Kinetics of sliding-window quantum error correction
abstract: Practical implementations of quantum error correction (QEC) require rapid measurement and continuous processing of the syndrome information in order to prevent a backlog of unprocessed data. While ``static'' QEC is theoretically well understood via mappings to equilibrium statistical mechanics models, such an understanding of ``real-time'' QEC is currently lacking. Here, we study the kinetics of sliding window decoding (SWD), an implementation of real-time decoding that acts on temporally local windows of noisy syndrome information and commits to corrections irreversibly at a nonzero rate. We propose an effective description of SWD in terms of a stochastic kinetic process, where $\mathbb{Z}_2$-charged point particles undergo parity-conserving reaction and diffusion. This model describes dynamics at length and time scales large compared to the window size $W$, whereas physics at scales smaller than $W$ leads to nontrivial $W$-dependent scaling of the effective parameters. We identify the rate of decoding $1/W$ as a relevant perturbation to the decodable phase. We also show broad applicability of our results by changing many microscopic details of SWD without affecting the effective description.
one_liner: Sliding-window QEC decoding is modeled as a stochastic reaction-diffusion process for real-time syndrome processing.
why_it_matters: It gives a kinetic theory for real-time QEC, where finite processing windows and irreversible correction timing can affect fault-tolerant performance.
detailed_summary: The paper studies the kinetics of sliding-window decoding, where noisy syndrome data are processed in finite temporal windows and corrections are committed irreversibly. It proposes an effective stochastic model in which Z2-charged point particles undergo parity-conserving reaction and diffusion at scales larger than the window size. The analysis identifies the decoding rate 1/W as a relevant perturbation and shows robustness of the effective description under changes to microscopic decoder details.
main_result: The work derives an effective kinetic description and scaling picture for sliding-window decoding in practical continuous QEC settings.
application_angle: It informs hardware control stacks that must decode syndromes continuously without data backlog in fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Long-lived memory effects in the defect bath of superconducting qubits
abstract: We reveal long-lived memory effects in the defect bath of a superconducting transmon qubit through electric-field tuning of two-level system (TLS) defects coupled to the qubit. Using a fast TLS mapping method we observe several hysteretic effects in the TLS environment with memory timescales of the order of seconds, far beyond the lifetimes of individual TLS defects. The observations can be explained by TLS coupling to electric field-polarised charge fluctuators in the defect bath. Our method enables detailed mapping of the dynamics of the bath's coupled microscopic degrees of freedom and the associated memory effects which can introduce temporally correlated noise. This information may be used to improve qubit-stabilisation and quantum error correction protocols.
one_liner: Fast TLS spectroscopy reveals seconds-long hysteresis and memory in the defect bath of a superconducting transmon qubit.
why_it_matters: Temporally correlated TLS-bath noise can undermine qubit stability and error correction, so resolving its microscopic dynamics is directly useful for hardware mitigation.
detailed_summary: The work uses electric-field tuning and fast TLS mapping to probe two-level-system defects coupled to a superconducting transmon. It observes hysteretic bath responses with memory lasting seconds, much longer than individual TLS lifetimes. The authors attribute the behavior to TLS coupling with electric-field-polarized charge fluctuators, providing a microscopic handle on correlated noise sources.
platform_or_system: superconducting transmon with TLS defect bath
main_result: The paper demonstrates direct observation and mapping of long-lived TLS-bath memory effects in a superconducting qubit environment.
application_angle: The measurements can inform qubit stabilization, calibration scheduling, and error-correction protocols that must account for correlated noise.

title: Programmable Heisenberg-limit sensor from a nonlinear quantum energy pump
abstract: We introduce a programmable Heisenberg-limited bosonic quantum sensor based on a nonlinear quantum energy pump, implemented with a Kerr-nonlinear resonator coupled to multiple high-Q microwave terminal resonators. For parameter estimation encoded in an arbitrary number-conserving Hamiltonian acting on the terminal modes, we analytically construct optimal sensing protocols that attain the maximal quantum Fisher information, including initial-state loading, probe preparation, and readout. For diagonal multiparameter signals, we further show that the full phase-sensing quantum Fisher information matrix can be obtained from correlations of locally measured physical terminal works, providing a signal-free calibration of the metrological resource. We numerically demonstrate the construction and its robustness using realistic circuit-QED parameters while including experimentally relevant imperfections.
one_liner: A Kerr nonlinear microwave energy pump is proposed as a programmable bosonic sensor reaching Heisenberg-limited scaling.
why_it_matters: It gives a circuit-QED route to optimal sensing protocols for broad number-conserving Hamiltonians rather than a single fixed signal model.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a nonlinear quantum energy pump built from a Kerr resonator coupled to multiple high-Q microwave terminal resonators. For arbitrary number-conserving Hamiltonian signals on the terminal modes, it analytically constructs optimal loading, probe-preparation, and readout protocols. For diagonal multiparameter phase sensing, it shows that locally measured terminal-work correlations can recover the full quantum Fisher information matrix, with numerical tests under realistic imperfections.
main_result: The main result is a programmable protocol family that attains maximal quantum Fisher information for bosonic parameter estimation.
application_angle: The architecture is relevant to microwave quantum sensors that need reconfigurable, calibrated, high-precision estimation across multiple signal channels.

title: Outdoor 100-m-scale air waveguides
abstract: Optical power densities for standoff spectroscopy, remote sensing, directed energy, and free-space optical communications are limited by diffraction and adverse atmospheric conditions such as turbulence, fog, and wind. Air waveguides, generated by ultrashort-pulsed laser filamentation, are a promising approach for transmission and collection of optical signals over long distances, overcoming beam diffraction and, for point-like sources, inverse square signal falloff with distance. In this work, we demonstrate outdoor guiding for the first time over a record length of ~100 m, exceeding the prior (indoor) record of 42 m. We correlate air waveguide performance to a range of real atmospheric conditions including turbulent refractive index structure parameter ($C_n^2$) values up to ~$2.5\times10^{-14} m^{-2/3}$, crosswind speeds up to ~2 m/s, as well as temperature, pressure, and humidity variations. Accompanying propagation simulations provide insight into the real effects of these environmental perturbations, particularly crosswind, on waveguide performance and lifetime. Our results pave the way for quasi-continuous air waveguiding with kHz-scale repetition rate filaments in challenging outdoor environments.
one_liner: Ultrashort-laser filamentation creates outdoor air waveguides that guide light over about 100 m under real atmospheric conditions.
why_it_matters: Long-range air guiding could improve remote optical delivery and collection where diffraction, turbulence, fog, and wind limit free-space links.
detailed_summary: The study demonstrates outdoor optical guiding over roughly 100 m using air waveguides generated by ultrashort-pulsed laser filamentation, exceeding the prior 42 m indoor record. It correlates guiding performance with turbulence strength, crosswind, temperature, pressure, and humidity. Simulations identify how environmental perturbations, especially crosswind, affect waveguide lifetime and performance.
main_result: The authors demonstrate record-length outdoor air waveguiding over approximately 100 m and characterize its atmospheric robustness.
application_angle: This advances practical beam delivery and signal collection for standoff spectroscopy, directed energy, remote sensing, and free-space optical communication.

title: Simultaneous Heisenberg-Limited Multiparameter Metrology via Indefinite Evolution
abstract: Quantum metrology achieves Heisenberg-limited precision in single-parameter estimation, but its multiparameter extension is fundamentally constrained by both parameter-encoding and measurement incompatibility. Noncommuting signal generators may cause incompatible parameter-encoding, preventing the quantum Fisher information matrix from simultaneously achieving the Heisenberg scale for all parameters. Due to incompatible optimal measurements, the classical Fisher information matrix represents the practical attainable precision. Here, we introduce a multiparameter metrology framework based on indefinite evolution (IE), in which different control operations and signal reversal are placed in a coherent superposition. For a single-qubit probe with mutually orthogonal signal generators, IE enables compatible parameter encoding and optimal measurement without the signal reversal. For parallel generators, where only signal reversal realized by its generator is available, IE can achieve the same performance. We further extend this mechanism to noisy, many-body, and high-dimensional probes, and establish general conditions for achieving the simultaneous Heisenberg-limit. In contrast, definite evolution cannot achieve the same performance under compatible optimal measurements, even when signal reversal is available. Our results identify IE as an operational resource for overcoming multiparameter incompatibility and open a route toward attainable Heisenberg-limited sensing in interferometric platforms.
one_liner: Indefinite evolution is proposed to make simultaneous multiparameter Heisenberg-limited sensing attainable despite incompatibility.
why_it_matters: It targets a central obstacle in practical quantum sensing: extracting multiple parameters at Heisenberg scaling with compatible encoding and measurement.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a metrology framework in which control operations and, when needed, signal reversal are placed in coherent superposition. For single-qubit probes with orthogonal generators, the method enables compatible parameter encoding and optimal measurement without signal reversal; for parallel generators, signal reversal can recover the same performance. The analysis extends to noisy, many-body, and high-dimensional probes and states general conditions for simultaneous Heisenberg-limited estimation.
platform_or_system: controlled quantum probes under indefinite evolution
main_result: The main result is a protocol framework that overcomes multiparameter incompatibility and achieves simultaneous Heisenberg-limit precision under specified conditions.
application_angle: It suggests implementable routes for interferometric and quantum-control sensors that must estimate several noncommuting or otherwise incompatible parameters.

title: Toward a Thermodynamic Framework for Dissipative Solitons: From Photonics to Turbulence and Bose--Einstein Condensate Analogies
abstract: Statistical reasoning in nonlinear optics follows three routes - wave-turbulence kinetics, multimode equilibrium thermodynamics, and mode-locking statistical mechanics -all relying on externally specified modal bases (waveguide, spectral window, or cavity bandwidth). We ask whether a dissipative soliton (DS) of the complex cubic-quintic Ginzburg-Landau equation provides a dynamically selected internal scale ratio as a coarse-graining variable. The DS generates its own spectral scales: localization bounds the spectrum, defining a fine-graining scale (cutoff) and a collective core scale; their dynamically selected ratio defines an emergent scale-separation index. This index acquires statistical meaning as an effective mode number only upon ensemble-coherence calibration--central novelty. Closed-form adiabatic spectra compress regimes onto a master diagram with entropy, internal energy, and energy-entropy slopes. DSR manifests as spectral core narrowing--intrinsic in normal dispersion, conditional in anomalous. Along normal dispersion, an entropy-proxy crossing precedes single-pulse loss, suggesting multipulse selection, though noise-driven transitions need testing. Along anomalous, no turnover occurs (path-dependent). Finite-time noise reveals a one-sided accessibility boundary inside the existence region; its role remains open. The deterministic pulse remains coherent; ratio not DOF count. Entropy decompositions are non-unique; temperature slope is not a state function; entropic multipulse selection is conjectural- each caveat is testable. Comparisons to wave turbulence, soliton gases, BEC, and negative-temperature states are outlined. Outcome: compact framework detailing DS coherence, stability, scaling, with experimental signatures and design criteria for chirped-pulse oscillators.
one_liner: A thermodynamic-style framework is proposed for dissipative soliton spectra using an internally selected scale-separation index.
why_it_matters: The framework links soliton coherence, stability, and pulse selection to measurable spectral signatures useful for nonlinear photonic oscillator design.
detailed_summary: The paper studies dissipative solitons of the complex cubic-quintic Ginzburg-Landau equation as systems that generate their own spectral coarse-graining scales. It defines a scale-separation index from the ratio between localization-limited spectral cutoff and collective core scale, then maps regimes using entropy, internal energy, and slope proxies. The analysis highlights normal- and anomalous-dispersion differences, possible multipulse selection signatures, and caveats such as nonunique entropy decompositions and the need for experimental calibration.
platform_or_system: dissipative soliton in nonlinear photonic oscillator models
main_result: The main result is a compact statistical framework that connects dynamically selected soliton spectral scales with coherence, stability, and design criteria.
application_angle: It may guide experiments and engineering choices for chirped-pulse oscillators and other dissipative nonlinear photonic systems.

title: How many labels can a biological oscillator carry? A quality-factor screen for proposed information carriers
abstract: How many distinguishable labels can a biological oscillator carry? Proposals invoking collective vibrational modes, endogenous electromagnetic fields, microtubule excitations and oscillatory phase codes are each debated on grounds particular to themselves, with no shared standard for comparison. We show that spectral distinguishability alone bounds the number of labels by the quality factor, M <= Q = 2 pi nu tau. This follows from the relation between linewidth and coherence time, so it is independent of substrate, of mechanism, and of any position on quantum effects in biology, and it can be evaluated from two published quantities. Applied to a recently proposed 30 GHz intracolumnar microwave field in cortex, it gives Q = 0.19: the linewidth exceeds the carrier five-fold. The obvious rescue, that a driven emitter can be spectrally narrower than its gain medium, requires a resonant cavity, and the model's own geometry forbids one. An independent bound on metabolic power is exceeded by five to nine orders of magnitude. Six further criteria follow from the same standpoint, including a two-sided persistence window requiring a label to be both readable and rewritable. Screening eleven carriers, only the low-frequency neural rhythms pass. High-frequency molecular carriers are eliminated by brevity, not by the fragility the debate has assumed.
one_liner: A quality-factor bound is used to screen how many distinguishable labels biological oscillators can physically carry.
why_it_matters: It offers a substrate-independent test for proposed high-frequency biological or quantum information carriers using coherence time and linewidth.
detailed_summary: The paper argues that the number of distinguishable spectral labels in a biological oscillator is bounded by its quality factor, M <= Q = 2 pi nu tau. Applying this to a proposed 30 GHz intracolumnar cortical microwave field gives Q = 0.19, implying a linewidth larger than the carrier frequency. It also evaluates cavity and metabolic-power constraints and screens eleven proposed carriers, finding only low-frequency neural rhythms pass the criteria.
main_result: The main result is a quality-factor screening rule that rejects several high-frequency molecular or electromagnetic biological label carriers on coherence grounds.
application_angle: The bound provides a practical filter for evaluating speculative bio-quantum sensing or information-processing mechanisms before detailed hardware models are pursued.

title: Stream Decoding with Confidence Scores at Room and Cryogenic Temperatures
abstract: In fault-tolerant quantum computing, fast and accurate decoding is crucial. Snowflake is a decoder for the surface code that runs in a streaming fashion. In this paper, we implement Snowflake on commercial FPGAs and validate them at room and cryogenic temperatures. Our results demonstrate high decoding throughput for small code distances that, when extrapolated, remains within acceptable limits for larger distances. Further, we incorporate the calculation of certain decoder confidence scores with negligible overhead both in terms of latency and physical resource utilisation. We note that implementing a large-scale system would require either a large FPGA beyond today's technology or clusters of FPGAs connected via a high-speed bus. Thus, we discuss an alternative architecture that exploits the locality of Snowflake by processing 2D slices of the 3D decoding window and offloading segments of the 3D structure to a high-speed memory.
one_liner: Snowflake surface-code decoding is implemented on commercial FPGAs and validated at both room and cryogenic temperatures.
why_it_matters: Low-latency cryogenic-compatible decoding is a key control-stack requirement for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.
detailed_summary: The paper implements the Snowflake streaming decoder for surface-code fault tolerance on commercial FPGA hardware. It validates operation at room and cryogenic temperatures, measuring throughput, latency, and resource use for small code distances. The authors add decoder confidence-score calculation with negligible latency and resource overhead, then discuss scaling limits and a locality-aware architecture using 2D slice processing plus high-speed memory.
main_result: The work demonstrates high-throughput Snowflake decoding with confidence scores on FPGAs, including cryogenic-temperature validation.
application_angle: It targets the real-time decoding layer needed to close the feedback loop in large fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Generating GKP states using quantum dots inside a strongly coupled cavity
abstract: GKP states enable fault-tolerant CV quantum computation, but their generation remains experimentally challenging due to their highly non-Gaussian and infinite-energy ideal structure. In this work, we present a realistic and scalable protocol for generating finite-energy resource states, specifically the qunaught state, using Schrodinger cat states generated in a strongly coupled quantum dot-cavity system. Our scheme combines deterministic squeezed cat-state generation, cat-breeding protocols, and homodyne measurements. Using numerical simulations, we analyze the role of various parameters of the quantum dot-cavity system in the generation of practical qunaught states. Furthermore, we quantify the trade-off between the fidelity and generation probability of these states and exploit the fact that accepting a structured set of homodyne outcomes can significantly enhance the overall success rate. The proposed approach is compatible with integrated photonics and telecom wavelengths, offering a promising route toward scalable CV quantum information processing.
one_liner: A quantum-dot cavity protocol is proposed for generating finite-energy GKP qunaught states via cat states and homodyne conditioning.
why_it_matters: It links solid-state cavity emitters to scalable continuous-variable fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing resources.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a realistic route to finite-energy GKP resource generation using Schrodinger cat states from a strongly coupled quantum dot-cavity system. The protocol combines deterministic squeezed cat generation, cat-breeding operations, and homodyne measurement selection. Numerical simulations quantify how device parameters affect qunaught-state fidelity and generation probability, including improved success rates from accepting structured homodyne outcomes.
main_result: The main result is a simulated, experimentally motivated protocol for producing practical qunaught GKP states from quantum-dot cavity cat states.
application_angle: Compatibility with integrated photonics and telecom wavelengths makes the approach relevant to scalable CV quantum processors and networks.

title: Nanoscale graphitization and defect evolution in silicon-vacancy center-containing nanodiamonds under high-pressure high-temperature annealing
abstract: Group-IV color centers, such as the silicon-vacancy (SiV) defect, are highly promising for solid-state quantum technologies. However, nanodiamonds typically exhibit significant lattice strain and structural disorder, which degrade their optical properties and hinder the resolution of the fine spectral structure at cryogenic temperatures. High-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) annealing offers a potential route to relax internal strain, although the phase stability of diamond at the nanoscale under such conditions remains poorly constrained. Here, we investigate the structural evolution of nanodiamonds during HPHT annealing using a Paris-Edinburgh press coupled with in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction at SOLEIL. A dedicated sample assembly combining nanodiamonds - NaCl - Pt enabled accurate pressure-temperature calibration and real-time monitoring of phase transformations. The diffraction data reveal that the onset of diamond-to-graphite transition occurs at approximately 1800 K at 2 GPa and 2120 K at 4 GPa under the applied HPHT heating protocol. These experimentally determined graphitization onsets define a practical pressure-temperature processing window for HPHT annealing of nanodiamonds while avoiding detectable graphitization and provide a calibrated framework for reliable off-beam annealing treatments that avoid graphitization. Photoluminescence measurements on samples annealed below the graphitization threshold show improved optical response, with partial resolution of the SiV fine structure at 12 K. These optical measurements suggest a relationship between nanoscale phase stability and the optical response of individual SiV-containing nanodiamonds following HPHT annealing. The experimentally established HPHT processing window provides a practical framework for the controlled processing of quantum nanodiamonds while avoiding graphitization.
one_liner: In situ synchrotron XRD maps HPHT graphitization thresholds for SiV nanodiamonds and links safer annealing to better optical spectra.
why_it_matters: Controlled nanodiamond processing can improve color-center optical quality without destroying the diamond phase.
detailed_summary: The study uses a Paris-Edinburgh press with in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction to track phase evolution in SiV-containing nanodiamonds under HPHT annealing. It identifies diamond-to-graphite onset near 1800 K at 2 GPa and 2120 K at 4 GPa for the tested protocol. Photoluminescence from samples annealed below the threshold shows improved optical response and partial SiV fine-structure resolution at 12 K.
main_result: The work establishes calibrated pressure-temperature processing windows that avoid detectable graphitization while improving SiV optical response.
application_angle: The result supports reproducible fabrication of quantum nanodiamonds for nanoscale photonics, sensing, and solid-state quantum devices.

title: Photonic realization of a subgraph extraction in a quantum random network
abstract: Understanding how complex connectivity emerges in networks is a fundamental challenge in classical and quantum science. In classical random networks, complex subgraphs typically require relatively high connection probabilities, whereas quantum random network theory predicts that such structures can arise at a single, lower threshold through entanglement and local operations. Here, using an integrated silicon photonic chip, we experimentally realize a quantum subgraph predicted by quantum random network theory in a four-node quantum random network. Our integrated platform exploits probabilistic photon-pair sources and coherent control of path modes to prepare a structured quantum subgraph through local transformations and postselection, operating in a threshold regime that differs from classical random networks. We verify that the subgraph state exhibits genuine high-dimensional multipartite entanglement across the nodes, providing experimental evidence that quantum entanglement enables connectivity structures beyond classical accessibility.
one_liner: An integrated silicon photonic chip realizes a four-node quantum random-network subgraph with high-dimensional multipartite entanglement.
why_it_matters: It experimentally probes network structures enabled by entanglement that are inaccessible at comparable classical random-network thresholds.
detailed_summary: The paper experimentally realizes a quantum subgraph predicted by quantum random network theory using an integrated silicon photonic chip. Probabilistic photon-pair sources and coherent path-mode control prepare the structured four-node state through local transformations and postselection. Measurements verify genuine high-dimensional multipartite entanglement across the network nodes.
platform_or_system: integrated silicon photonic quantum network chip
main_result: The main result is photonic realization and verification of an entangled subgraph in a four-node quantum random network.
application_angle: The experiment is relevant to scalable quantum communication networks where entanglement changes achievable connectivity and routing structures.

title: Quantum Theory of Third-harmonic Generation in Epsilon-Near-Zero Materials
abstract: We present a theoretical framework, based on the Green's tensor quantization method, to describe third-harmonic generation in epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) materials and derive analytical, closed-form solutions for the generation efficiency. We validate our model against experimental measurements of wavelength- and angle-resolved third-harmonic generation efficiency from 30 nm-thin ITO nanolayers at low pump intensity, described under the undepleted pump approximation. Our results provide a local and scalar effective model for quantum nonlinear processes in dispersive and lossy ENZ media, and establishes a simple and reliable framework for investigating a variety of nonlinear optical phenomena with applications to quantum sensing, quantum information, and quantum nondemolition measurements.
one_liner: A Green-tensor quantum model gives closed-form third-harmonic generation efficiencies for lossy epsilon-near-zero nanolayers.
why_it_matters: A validated quantum nonlinear-optics model helps design ENZ media for sensing, information processing, and nondemolition measurements.
detailed_summary: The paper develops a Green's tensor quantization framework for third-harmonic generation in dispersive and lossy epsilon-near-zero materials. It derives analytical closed-form generation-efficiency expressions under the undepleted pump approximation. The model is validated against wavelength- and angle-resolved measurements from 30 nm ITO nanolayers at low pump intensity.
main_result: The work provides a validated local scalar effective model for quantum third-harmonic generation in ENZ media.
application_angle: It gives device designers a compact framework for ENZ-based nonlinear quantum sensing, information, and measurement platforms.

title: Rf beam steering using on-ohip optical true time delay on 3 micrometer siliocn on insulator platfrom
abstract: We present the design, packaging, and system-level experimental demonstration of a reconfigurable 5-bit, 4-channel optical true time delay (OTTD) chip realized on a 3 micrometer thick silicon on insulator (SOI) platform at VTT. The chip enables 32 discrete delay states over a 0 to 101 picoseconds range, with a delay resolution of 3.25 picoseconds, making it well suited for broadband RF beamforming with upcoming 6G FR3 band systems around 10 GHz. Each channel incorporates five binary weighted delay stages controlled by Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) based thermo-optic switches with an extinction ratio exceeding 25 decibels and an average switching power of 25 milliwatts. The chip is embedded within an analog radio-over-fibre (A-RoF) link, and the outputs are connected to a PCB-based four-element patch antenna array. Accurate RF beam steering is demonstrated at broadside and at 30 degrees from broadside using a 16 - QAM signal modulated at 100 MBaud on a 10 GHz carrier. An error vector magnitude (EVM) degradation of approximately 1 percent is observed upon steering, and an extinction ratio exceeding 50 decibels is measured between the two receiver positions. The results confirm the potential of integrated OTTD technology for compact, power-efficient, and broadband beamforming in next-generation wireless and radar systems.
one_liner: A 5-bit four-channel silicon photonic true-time-delay chip demonstrates broadband RF beam steering with low EVM penalty.
why_it_matters: Integrated optical delay lines can shrink and improve broadband beamforming hardware for wireless, radar, and photonic RF systems.
detailed_summary: The paper reports design, packaging, and system-level testing of a reconfigurable 5-bit, four-channel optical true time delay chip on a 3 micrometer SOI platform. The device provides 32 delay states spanning 0 to 101 ps with 3.25 ps resolution using MZI thermo-optic switches. Integrated into an analog radio-over-fibre link and four-element patch antenna array, it steers a 16-QAM 10 GHz signal to broadside and 30 degrees with about 1 percent EVM degradation.
main_result: The system demonstrates chip-based RF beam steering at 10 GHz with high receiver-position extinction and modest modulation-quality penalty.
application_angle: The hardware points toward compact broadband beamforming modules for 6G FR3 links, phased arrays, and radar front ends.

title: Projection measurement of the comb basis through free-electron-photon interactions
abstract: Free electrons, driven by rapid advances in photon-induced near-field electron microscopy, have emerged as a promising platform for quantum information processing, including quantum computing and quantum sensing. However, conventional measurements that rely on the electron energy loss spectrum (EELS) are inherently destructive to electron qubits, thereby constraining their applicability. In this Letter, we propose a scheme that performs projection measurement on the electron comb basis, where high measurement precision can be achieved with bright squeezed vacuum states and strong PINEM couplings. Notably, this approach is not only nondestructive to electron qubits but also maximally incompatible with energy measurements, enabling alternative quantum information applications, such as quantum error mitigation and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering detection. Our findings open an avenue towards a systematic understanding of quantum free electrons and towards the development of nondestructive free electron quantum information tasks.
one_liner: Proposes nondestructive projection measurement of free-electron comb-basis qubits using photon-mediated PINEM interactions.
why_it_matters: A nondestructive readout channel could make free-electron qubits more useful for quantum sensing, error mitigation, and nonclassical-correlation tests.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a projection-measurement protocol for free-electron comb-basis states using free-electron-photon interactions rather than conventional EELS. Bright squeezed vacuum states and strong PINEM coupling are predicted to give high measurement precision while avoiding destruction of the electron qubit. Because the measurement is maximally incompatible with energy readout, it also enables protocols such as error mitigation and EPR-steering detection.
main_result: The main result is a proposed nondestructive comb-basis projection measurement with enhanced precision from squeezed light and strong electron-photon coupling.
application_angle: Practical relevance lies in extending free-electron quantum information and sensing beyond destructive energy-spectrum readout.

title: Boosting self hybridized exciton polaritons with metal clad WS2 waveguides
abstract: The formation of Fabry Perot and guided wave self hybridized exciton polaritons in two dimensional materials results in long range exciton energy transfer and strong exciton exciton interactions. Here, we demonstrate that the coupling strength between photonic modes and excitons is significantly boosted by embedding the active excitonic layer in a metal clad WS2 waveguide. The photonic modes in this waveguide exhibit modified dispersion properties for both Fabry Perot type and guided wave exciton polaritons compared to pure WS2 flakes, and show an increased couplingr strength. Our results provide a robust approach for controlling exciton photon interactions and their coupling strength in hybrid heterostructures.
one_liner: Demonstrates stronger self-hybridized exciton-polariton coupling in metal-clad WS2 waveguides.
why_it_matters: Boosted exciton-photon coupling in 2D-material waveguides offers a tunable route to polaritonic devices with long-range energy transfer and nonlinear interactions.
detailed_summary: The work embeds an active WS2 layer in a metal-clad waveguide to modify photonic dispersion and strengthen exciton-photon coupling. It studies both Fabry-Perot-type and guided-wave self-hybridized exciton polaritons relative to bare WS2 flakes. The reported architecture provides a practical heterostructure approach for engineering polariton mode structure and coupling strength.
main_result: The main result is enhanced coupling strength between WS2 excitons and waveguide photonic modes in a metal-clad geometry.
application_angle: The platform is relevant for compact polaritonic photonic components, exciton transport, and nonlinear 2D-material optoelectronics.

title: A Quantum Dynamics Tutorial: Visualising Dynamical Decoupling Sequences on the Bloch Sphere
abstract: Dynamical decoupling protocols provide a versatile toolbox for robust control of quantum systems, suppressing noise that would otherwise limit their performance. This tutorial aims to provide an intuitive interpretation of these protocols. Written from an experimentalist's perspective, we use the Bloch sphere picture to visualise quantum dynamics for a range of sequences. Here each dynamical decoupling operation can be viewed as an "effective field vector", whilst the phase and population of the two-level system is encoded into a "Bloch vector". The two-level dynamics are calculated by the cross product between these two vectors, such that the quantum state represented by the Bloch vector rotates around the effective field vector. Several prominent control schemes are simulated using this picture, starting with a Rabi oscillation, followed by the Ramsey sequence and a selection of pulsed and continuous dynamical decoupling techniques. These sequences are engineered to preserve control of the quantum system for as long as possible, with their efficacy often quantified by a coherence time. We clarify the definition of the longitudinal $T_1$, transverse $T_2$ and inhomogeneous $T_2^*$ coherence times, which are used across the literature. Each simulation has an accompanying animation to illustrate the protocol's two-level dynamics on the Bloch sphere. The custom simulation and Bloch sphere plotting scripts are also provided in an open access repository to allow the reader to reproduce, modify, and explore these results. Dynamical decoupling sequences have established themselves as an invaluable tool across the entire quantum technologies remit; by providing an open framework alongside this tutorial, we aim to make these protocols more accessible to new researchers discovering this thriving field.
one_liner: Presents an experimentalist-focused Bloch-sphere tutorial and open simulations for dynamical decoupling protocols.
why_it_matters: Clear, reproducible control visualizations can accelerate training and protocol design across quantum sensing, photonics, and hardware experiments.
detailed_summary: This tutorial frames two-level quantum control using Bloch vectors and effective field vectors, with dynamics generated by their cross product. It simulates Rabi oscillations, Ramsey sequences, and pulsed and continuous dynamical decoupling schemes while clarifying T1, T2, and T2* conventions. Accompanying open scripts and animations make the control sequences reproducible and modifiable.
main_result: The main result is an open tutorial framework for visualizing and simulating key dynamical decoupling sequences on the Bloch sphere.
application_angle: It is practically useful for onboarding experimentalists and designing coherence-preserving control in sensors, qubits, and photonic quantum systems.

title: Quantum Signatures of Two-Electron HBT Interference in Free Space
abstract: Understanding how fermionic exchange and Coulomb repulsion jointly shape two-electron correlations is essential for identifying genuine quantum signatures in multi-electron interference experiments. To address this interplay, we investigate Hanbury Brown and Twiss interference of two electrons generated by two independent needle-tip emitters within a full quantum-mechanical framework. In the absence of Coulomb interaction, the approach reproduces the results previously obtained within a quantum path formalism. For Coulomb-interacting electrons, we predict characteristic features absent in a semiclassical description: a pronounced Coulomb-dominated suppression region as well as Coulomb-induced phase offsets and fringe shifts. At the same time, outside of the Coulomb-dominated region, the spatial oscillation frequency is essentially governed by fermionic exchange symmetry. Our results establish quantitative parameter regimes for disentangling Coulomb interaction from fermionic exchange symmetry in such experiments.
one_liner: Predicts free-space two-electron HBT interference signatures separating fermionic exchange from Coulomb effects.
why_it_matters: Quantitative regimes for isolating exchange-driven correlations can guide electron-interference experiments and fermionic quantum-optics tests.
detailed_summary: The paper models Hanbury Brown and Twiss interference from two independent needle-tip electron emitters in a full quantum-mechanical treatment. Without Coulomb interaction, it recovers prior quantum-path results; with interaction, it predicts suppression regions plus phase offsets and fringe shifts absent semiclassically. Away from the Coulomb-dominated region, spatial oscillation frequency remains governed mainly by fermionic exchange symmetry.
main_result: The main result is a set of predicted quantum-correlation signatures that distinguish Coulomb repulsion from fermionic exchange in two-electron HBT experiments.
application_angle: The analysis supports precision design of electron interferometry platforms for quantum-coherence and correlation measurements.

title: Verifying full quantum network nonlocality in arbitrary configurations by nonlinear Bell-like inequalities
abstract: Full quantum network nonlocality (FQNN) describes a scenario where all sources in a network are nonlocal. Existing criteria of FQNN can only be verified in star networks by violating a single Bell-like inequality. Here we propose a method that certifies FQNN in general quantum networks using only a single Bell-like inequality. We show that the topological obstacle to one-shot detection can be overcome by expanding the original network with a carefully chosen number of auxiliary local sources and parties. The correlations of the enlarged network are then tested with a single inequality; a violation implies that all original sources must be nonlocal. Our approach provides an efficient, experimentally friendly way to verify FQNN in any network topology.
one_liner: Introduces a single nonlinear Bell-like inequality method to certify full quantum network nonlocality in arbitrary topologies.
why_it_matters: Topology-independent FQNN verification could simplify experimental certification of multi-source quantum networks beyond star configurations.
detailed_summary: The paper addresses full quantum network nonlocality, where every source in a network must be nonlocal. It proposes enlarging an arbitrary network with auxiliary local sources and parties so that one nonlinear Bell-like inequality can certify the original network. A violation in the enlarged network implies all original sources are nonlocal, removing the star-network limitation of previous criteria.
main_result: The main result is a one-shot Bell-like certification method for full quantum network nonlocality across general network configurations.
application_angle: This gives quantum-communication experiments a more scalable route to verifying genuinely nonlocal multi-source network resources.

title: Universal scaling of spatially extended zero modes in inhomogeneous SSH chains
abstract: Protected zero modes are a hallmark of topological phases of matter and are exponentially localized at sharp interfaces between distinct gapped phases. We investigate how this picture changes for smooth interfaces in a broad class of inhomogeneous Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) models. Combining an exact lattice solution with an inhomogeneous Dirac description, we show that the associated Jackiw-Rebbi zero mode becomes spatially extended. For arbitrary smooth hopping profiles, its lattice extension universally scales as the square root of the system size, independently of the microscopic details of the interface. This emergent length defines a mesoscopic critical region separating two gapped phases, within which correlations decay algebraically before crossing over to exponential decay. In addition, the entanglement entropy scales as the logarithm of the emergent length near the interface, confirming the interpretation of a mesoscopic critical region. Our results establish a universal critical length governing the low-energy physics of smooth topological interfaces.
one_liner: Shows that smooth interfaces in inhomogeneous SSH chains produce zero modes whose extent scales universally as the square root of system size.
why_it_matters: Universal scaling of topological-interface modes informs engineered photonic and quantum-simulator lattices with deliberately graded couplings.
detailed_summary: The work combines an exact lattice solution with an inhomogeneous Dirac description for broad classes of smooth-interface SSH models. Instead of exponential localization at a sharp boundary, the Jackiw-Rebbi zero mode becomes spatially extended with a lattice length scaling as the square root of system size. The emergent mesoscopic critical region shows algebraic correlations and logarithmic entanglement-entropy scaling near the interface.
main_result: The main result is a universal square-root system-size scaling law for spatially extended zero modes at smooth topological interfaces.
application_angle: The result is relevant to designing topological modes in photonic waveguide arrays, cold-atom lattices, and other quantum-simulation hardware.

title: Quantum Coordination Advantages in AI State-Tracking Tasks: Semantic Compilation and Latent Memory
abstract: We prove inference-time quantum coordination advantages for specified AI state-tracking tasks. A solver compresses semantic history into a future-accessible boundary state and later answers a query. We count communication $B$, persistent instance-dependent memory $M$, and local work $D$; classical recurrence, caches, tools, and recomputation are allowed and charged. The central result is a boundary-preserving semantic-compilation theorem. It maps a finite one-way, streaming, or adaptive causal task into a semantic AI interface while preserving event order and access to past input. Classical boundary-state lower bounds and quantum-memory upper bounds transfer up to explicit compiler overhead, independently of the finite-precision recurrent architecture. Two applications have classical semantics. Matched-entity synopsis QA inherits the hidden-matching separation between $O(\log N)$ qubits and $Ω(\sqrt{N})$ classical boundary bits. Continual requirements auditing inherits a Max-$k$SAT streaming separation: a recurrent solver uses $O(\log^5 n\log(1/δ))$ qubits and polylogarithmic classical workspace to obtain a $0.7172$-approximation, whereas every classical one-pass finite-information solver attaining that ratio requires $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ coordination width. As a quantum-native compiler test, a stabilizer latent-state dialogue uses $n$ qubits, while every exact finite-state classical causal online realization satisfies $B+M \ge \frac{1}{2}n^2+(\frac{3}{2}-\log_2 3)n+O(1)$. The source protocols, streaming algorithms, and stabilizer witness are imported; the new result is their architecture-independent semantic transfer. These are memory and coordination separations, not runtime or empirical advantages for present-day language models. The stabilizer result assumes exact simulation and ideal noiseless quantum memory.
one_liner: Shows formal quantum memory and coordination advantages for semantic AI state-tracking tasks via boundary-preserving compilation.
why_it_matters: It connects quantum communication complexity separations to AI-style state tracking, clarifying where quantum memory could matter beyond runtime speedups.
detailed_summary: The paper proves a boundary-preserving semantic-compilation theorem mapping one-way, streaming, and adaptive causal tasks into AI state-tracking interfaces. Known classical lower bounds and quantum-memory upper bounds transfer with explicit overhead, yielding separations for synopsis QA, requirements auditing, and stabilizer latent-state dialogue. The claims are architectural and information-theoretic, assuming ideal quantum memory rather than near-term empirical LLM speedups.
main_result: Finite causal tasks can be compiled into semantic AI interfaces while preserving quantum-versus-classical boundary-state separations.
application_angle: The work frames quantum memory as a future resource for compact long-horizon state tracking and coordination in AI-like workflows.

title: Assessing fidelity-limiting factors and achieving single-qubit gate fidelity beyond 99.999% in driven silicon spin qubits
abstract: In semiconductor single-spin qubits, high-fidelity quantum gates have been demonstrated; however, achieving consistent performance remains challenging due to variations in driven qubit coherence, which is less explored than free-evolution coherence such as $T_2^*$. Here, we report single-qubit gate fidelities above 99.999%, achieved by dramatically extending the driven-spin coherence time and suppressing off-resonant driving effects that are detrimental to accurate fidelity benchmarking. We demonstrate that removing proximal reservoirs significantly enhances the spin-locking coherence time ($T_{1ρ}$), a critical metric for qubits under microwave driving. Furthermore, we reveal that in typical spin qubit setups using parity readout and rectangular pulses, off-resonant excitation of neighboring qubits causes substantial benchmarking artifacts. By optimizing device conditions to mitigate microwave-induced degradation and implementing spectrally tailored pulse shaping, we achieve a $π/2$ gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%, with remaining errors primarily limited by incoherent noise. These results showcase the mechanisms that bound fidelity benchmarking in state-of-the-art silicon spin qubits and provide practical guidelines for achieving and verifying high fidelities in these systems.
one_liner: Reports silicon spin-qubit single-qubit gate fidelity above 99.999% by improving driven coherence and suppressing benchmark artifacts.
why_it_matters: It identifies practical fidelity limiters in driven silicon spin qubits and gives device and pulse-design guidance for reproducible high-fidelity gates.
detailed_summary: The authors study fidelity-limiting mechanisms in driven semiconductor spin qubits, focusing on spin-locking coherence rather than only free-evolution metrics. Removing proximal reservoirs extends driven-spin coherence, while spectrally tailored pulses reduce off-resonant excitation of neighboring qubits during parity-readout benchmarking. The optimized system reaches a pi/2 gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%, with residual errors mainly attributed to incoherent noise.
main_result: A pi/2 single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)% is demonstrated after mitigating microwave-induced degradation and off-resonant driving.
application_angle: The result strengthens silicon spin qubits as a scalable hardware platform and improves confidence in benchmarking ultra-high-fidelity control.

title: Physics-Constrained Compressed Sensing for Quantum Sensing in the Data-Starved Regime
abstract: Quantum sensors promise measurement sensitivities that can scale at the Heisenberg limit, but in practice their performance is often degraded by noise, finite sampling, and implementation imperfections. In this work we present a general framework for improving parameter estimation in such settings by exploiting intrinsic structural constraints of time-domain correlation functions. Our approach builds on the observation of Kemper et al. [PRL 132, 160403 (2024)] that two-time correlation functions of Hermitian observables generate Gram matrices that are positive semidefinite, a property that can be violated in experimentally acquired data. We formulate signal reconstruction as a convex optimization problem that enforces positive semidefiniteness, Toeplitz structure, and low-rank priors motivated by the underlying dynamics. We show analytically that, under suitable conditions, the ground-truth signal can be uniquely identified in the noiseless case and recovered stably in the presence of noise. We further demonstrate numerically, in a GHZ-based magnetometry protocol, that enforcing these physical constraints can significantly improve frequency estimation from sparse and noisy data. In particular, we observe a clear advantage in the data-starved regime, where only a small number of time samples are available and standard spectral estimation methods, including matrix pencil techniques, provide limited or unstable improvement over direct fitting. While the reconstructed signals do not in general reach the shot-noise-limited performance, the proposed approach consistently reduces estimation error and recovers much of the underlying structure of the signal. These results indicate that incorporating universal physical constraints into data analysis can enhance the practical performance of quantum sensing protocols without requiring additional hardware resources or calibration.
one_liner: Introduces physics-constrained compressed sensing to improve quantum-sensor parameter estimation from sparse noisy correlation data.
why_it_matters: It boosts sensing performance in data-starved experiments using analysis constraints rather than added hardware, sampling, or calibration overhead.
detailed_summary: The paper formulates time-domain quantum-sensing reconstruction as a convex optimization problem enforcing positive semidefinite Gram structure, Toeplitz symmetry, and low-rank dynamical priors. It proves uniqueness in ideal conditions and stable recovery under noise assumptions. Numerical GHZ magnetometry examples show improved frequency estimation when only sparse, noisy time samples are available, outperforming unstable standard spectral methods in that regime.
main_result: Physics-constrained reconstruction reduces frequency-estimation error from sparse noisy quantum-sensor data in simulations.
application_angle: The approach can improve practical sensor readout pipelines without changing the quantum sensor hardware.

title: High-dimensional Supermode Photonics Enabled by Hierarchical Supersymmetric Transformation
abstract: Modes provide a fundamental degree of freedom for photonic information processing, yet conventional multimode waveguides exhibit non-equidistant effective-index distributions, making closely spaced modes vulnerable to intermodal crosstalk. Supermode photonics can overcome this limitation by geometrically engineering coupled waveguide arrays to realize large and equidistant effective-index spacing, but precise supermode excitation and detection remain challenging at the subwavelength scale. Here, we report a hierarchical second-order discrete supersymmetric (DSUSY) transformation method that enables high-purity excitation and extraction of arbitrary target supermodes in a compact and scalable architecture. We experimentally demonstrate six-supermode multiplexing systems on silicon-on-insulator and silicon nitride platforms. Benefiting from the large supermode index spacing and the isospectrality of DSUSY transformations, the fabricated devices exhibit low insertion losses (<2.6 dB) and intermodal crosstalk (<-11.1 dB) for all channels over a 100-nm wavelength range. A high-speed transmission experiment on the silicon device achieves an aggregate data rate of 1.2 Tbit/s, with all channel bit error rates below the 7% hard-decision forward-error-correction threshold. The method can further support polarization-insensitive architectures, enabling compact polarization-supermode hybrid multiplexing. This work provides a scalable route toward high-dimensional supermode photonics for high-capacity optical interconnects, highly parallel AI optical computing, and high-dimensional quantum information processing.
one_liner: Demonstrates scalable six-supermode multiplexing on SOI and SiN using hierarchical supersymmetric photonic transformations.
why_it_matters: It offers a compact route to high-dimensional, low-crosstalk photonic channels for optical interconnects, computing, and quantum information.
detailed_summary: The work uses hierarchical second-order discrete supersymmetric transformations to engineer coupled-waveguide arrays for high-purity excitation and extraction of target supermodes. Six-supermode multiplexers are fabricated on silicon-on-insulator and silicon nitride platforms, showing insertion loss below 2.6 dB and crosstalk below -11.1 dB over 100 nm. A silicon-device transmission test reaches 1.2 Tbit/s aggregate throughput with all channels below the 7% HD-FEC threshold.
platform_or_system: SOI and silicon nitride coupled-waveguide arrays
main_result: Six-supermode multiplexing with low loss, low crosstalk, and 1.2 Tbit/s aggregate transmission is experimentally demonstrated.
application_angle: The architecture supports dense optical links and may extend to high-dimensional quantum photonic encoding.

title: Robust CHSH Self-Testing with Finite-Energy GKP States
abstract: We present a full-oscillator analysis of a finite-energy GKP CHSH test whose observed score yields robust Bell-pair self-testing. Periodically binned position and momentum give the Pauli settings, while a fixed binary coarse-graining of photon number modulo four and its displaced conjugate realize the tilted settings. For a number-filtered GKP source, we retain the finite codeword overlap, define the measurements on all photon-number sectors, and compute the physical correlations without logical post-corrections. With the canonical ideal-logical displacement \(d=\sqrtπ\), the CHSH value exceeds the local bound above \(4.56\) dB of per-peak squeezing, and Kaniewski's extractability bound becomes nontrivial above \(5.02\) dB. Calibrating only \(d\) using an independently characterized finite-energy parameter lowers these model thresholds to \(4.21\) dB and \(4.58\) dB, respectively; at \(12\) dB, it raises the score from \(2.69486\) to \(2.78858\) and the corresponding target-state overlap bound from \(0.90758\) to \(0.97243\). This calibration is fixed before Bell-test data are collected. The displacement activates the odd modulo-four sectors, so their fixed a priori assignments are a genuine finite-energy component. The large gain is specific to the deterministic phase-bit coarse-graining; independently calibrating the one-bit POVM with randomized odd-sector outcomes gives only a much smaller improvement. These are honest-model predictions, not loss, detection-efficiency, or finite-sample thresholds. In an experiment, a device-independent guarantee for an extracted Bell pair follows by inserting a confidence lower bound on the observed CHSH score into the self-testing theorem.
one_liner: Analyzes finite-energy GKP CHSH tests that can robustly self-test Bell pairs using realistic oscillator measurements.
why_it_matters: It gives concrete squeezing thresholds and calibration choices for turning finite-energy GKP photonic states into device-independent certificates.
detailed_summary: The paper provides a full-oscillator treatment of CHSH self-testing with finite-energy GKP states, including codeword overlap and all photon-number sectors. Periodically binned quadratures define Pauli settings, while photon-number modulo-four coarse-graining and displaced measurements realize tilted settings. Calibrating the displacement using an independently characterized finite-energy parameter lowers model thresholds and improves the 12 dB predicted extractability bound from 0.90758 to 0.97243.
main_result: Finite-energy GKP Bell tests can yield nontrivial robust self-testing bounds above model squeezing thresholds near 4.6 to 5.0 dB.
application_angle: The analysis informs experimental designs for device-independent certification in bosonic photonic quantum communication and computing.

title: Quantum Codes with Arbitrary Z-Rotation logical Gates and Applications to Fault-Tolerant Code Switching
abstract: A technique for realizing a universal set of fault-tolerant quantum operations is the code switching method, which leverages two quantum codes with complementary sets of transversal gates. To date, the application of this technique has been largely limited to families of color codes supporting a logical $T$ gate. No analogous code switching protocols exist for many other prominent families, such as rotated surface codes, or for finer $Z$-rotation gates. In this work, we first utilize the doubling technique as a unified framework to construct a class of quantum color codes encoding a single logical qubit with an arbitrarily large minimum distance, enabling the transversal realization of arbitrary small logical $Z$-rotation gates. We investigate the structural properties of this code family, demonstrating that they improve upon the parameters of state-of-the-art triorthogonal codes, achieve lower qubit overhead compared to certain known color codes, and admit single-shot decoding of $Z$-syndromes via meta-checks. Furthermore, we show that this framework extends beyond color codes; specifically, it enables the generation of $r$-orthogonal quantum codes, $r \ge 2$, that inherit the local geometry of rotated surface codes. We then provide an overhead optimization protocol alongside several candidate codes tailored for realizing logical $Z$-rotation gates within rotated surface codes. Finally, we extend the fault-tolerant code switching protocol based on transversal CNOT gates to incorporate fault-tolerant realization of $Z$-rotation gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy for geometries compatible with rotated surface codes. We present the first demonstration of fault-tolerant magic state preparation by means of code switching within a distance-three rotated surface code using a total footprint of only 45 physical qubits, and evaluate its performance through a simulation.
one_liner: Constructs quantum codes with arbitrary transversal Z rotations and applies them to fault-tolerant code switching for surface-code geometries.
why_it_matters: It expands code switching beyond T-gate color-code settings and targets lower-overhead fault-tolerant rotations for practical architectures.
detailed_summary: The paper uses a doubling framework to build single-logical-qubit color-code families with arbitrarily large distance and transversal small logical Z rotations. It also generates r-orthogonal codes that retain rotated-surface-code local geometry and proposes overhead-optimized switching protocols for Clifford-hierarchy Z rotations. A distance-three rotated-surface-code example prepares a magic state fault tolerantly with a 45-physical-qubit footprint and is evaluated in simulation.
platform_or_system: color and rotated surface quantum codes
main_result: The authors demonstrate simulated fault-tolerant magic-state preparation by code switching in a distance-three rotated surface code using 45 physical qubits.
application_angle: These constructions could reduce overhead for implementing non-Clifford logical rotations in surface-code-based quantum processors.

title: Impact of strain and dark states on spectroscopic measurements of silicon-vacancy centers in diamond
abstract: Negatively charged silicon-vacancy (SiV$^-$) centers in diamond offer an attractive platform for the development of many forms of quantum technology. However, questions remain in connection to how large ensembles of SiV$^-$ centers behave in concert. Here, we develop a computational model designed to simulate recent experiments where optical multidimensional coherent spectroscopy (MDCS) was used to examine a high-concentration sample of SiV$^-$ centers in diamond, revealing significant variations in spectral signature depending on the detection scheme. Simulation results reveal that strain effects are highly random in this system, with a characteristic axial strain of $2.8 \times 10^{-4}$ and a shear strain of $3.5 \times 10^{-5}$. They suggest in addition that highly strained centers (with values exceeding $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$) may become significantly decoupled from optical emission. The results have implications for the use of SiV$^-$ centers as quantum sensors.
one_liner: Models how random strain and dark-state formation reshape ensemble SiV- spectroscopy in diamond under MDCS readout.
why_it_matters: Clarifies why dense SiV- ensembles show detection-dependent spectra, a key issue for using them as robust solid-state quantum sensors.
detailed_summary: The paper builds a computational model for multidimensional coherent spectroscopy of high-concentration negatively charged silicon-vacancy centers in diamond. Simulations indicate highly random strain, with characteristic axial strain of 2.8e-4 and shear strain of 3.5e-5. The model further suggests that sufficiently strained centers can decouple strongly from optical emission, changing the apparent ensemble spectrum under different detection schemes.
main_result: The study extracts realistic random strain scales and identifies strain-induced optical darkening as a mechanism behind MDCS spectral variations.
application_angle: Understanding strain and dark-state effects helps engineer SiV- diamond samples and readout protocols for quantum sensing.

title: Statistically-Secure Bit Commitment and Coin Flipping Protocols Based on Quantum Hardware Assumptions
abstract: Bit commitment is impossible to achieve with unconditional security, even in quantum cryptogra- phy. We show that statistically secure bit commitment, satisfying both hiding and binding, can be constructed from hybrid locked physical unclonable functions (HLPUFs), a hardware primitive that combines classical hardware tokens and quantum communication. Our protocol uses these hardware assumptions in a novel and non-trivial way to achieve the first mistrustful two-party cryptographic protocol based on hybrid hardware modules. We prove statistical hiding and binding under natu- ral assumptions on the HLPUF and using a carefully designed challenge generation algorithm as a subroutine of our bit-commitment protocol. The construction also yields the first hardware-based coin-flipping protocol. Our results suggest a new paradigm for secure two-party cryptography in quantum networks, combining rigorous security guarantees with a concrete route toward practical implementation.
one_liner: Proposes statistically secure bit commitment and coin flipping from hybrid locked physical unclonable functions.
why_it_matters: It gives a hardware-assumption route to mistrustful two-party cryptography for quantum networks, beyond standard communication-only protocols.
detailed_summary: The work constructs statistically hiding and binding bit commitment using hybrid locked physical unclonable functions that combine classical hardware tokens with quantum communication. A challenge-generation subroutine is used to enforce the security properties under natural assumptions on the HLPUF. The same construction yields a hardware-based coin-flipping protocol.
main_result: The paper demonstrates the first mistrustful two-party cryptographic protocol based on hybrid hardware modules with statistical security guarantees.
application_angle: It points to deployable quantum-network cryptography built from physical hardware assumptions rather than idealized unconditional security.

title: Floquet Green's functions for lattice electrons driven by Gaussian quantum light
abstract: We formulate Floquet Green's functions for noninteracting single-band lattice electrons driven by a reservoir-stabilized single-mode Gaussian quantum light source. The source is prescribed externally and is not updated by the many-electron polarization, while an active electronic probe still conditions the source evolution through the Peierls coupling. The two time arguments of a Green's function share one source history: the lesser and greater components are obtained by convolving a shared-history four-endpoint kernel with the continuous bath kernels before the final source trace, while the bath canonical anticommutation relation yields an equal-time covariance that seeds the retarded and advanced one-leg propagations. The Peierls coupling is treated nonperturbatively within the prescribed-source model, and classical Floquet theory is recovered in the appropriate limit. Numerical calculations on a minimal one-dimensional model show finite-coupling quantum-source corrections beyond a prescribed classical drive, together with spectral reconstruction and occupancy redistribution for squeezed vacuum and squeezed coherent sources. The squeezing parameter and phase provide additional control knobs, beyond classical amplitude modulation, for both sideband structure and occupied weight. This work provides a theoretical framework for quantum Floquet engineering of condensed matter with an externally prescribed quantum light source.
one_liner: Develops Floquet Green's functions for lattice electrons driven by externally prescribed Gaussian quantum light.
why_it_matters: Provides a framework for quantum-light control of electronic spectra beyond classical Floquet driving, relevant to photonic materials engineering.
detailed_summary: The paper formulates a shared-history Floquet Green's-function approach for noninteracting lattice electrons driven by a reservoir-stabilized single-mode Gaussian quantum light source. The Peierls coupling is treated nonperturbatively within a prescribed-source model, while classical Floquet theory is recovered in the appropriate limit. Numerical one-dimensional examples show quantum-source corrections, spectral reconstruction, and occupancy redistribution for squeezed vacuum and squeezed coherent drives.
platform_or_system: lattice electrons driven by Gaussian quantum light
main_result: The work shows that squeezing strength and phase can tune sidebands and occupied spectral weight beyond classical amplitude modulation.
application_angle: The formalism supports quantum Floquet engineering of materials using structured quantum photonic sources.

title: Spin-coherent quantum designs
abstract: Coherent states bridge the gap between quantum and classical physics, but their overcomplete and nonorthogonal nature makes it difficult to identify the minimal discrete set needed to reconstruct quantum information. Finite spin-coherent tomography and discrete coherent-state operator bases are known, but here we address the more specific rank-resolved problem of preserving the canonical contravariant-symbol representation. We show that the canonical finite coherent-state formula reconstructs every operator in the rank-$S$ sector exactly if and only if the sampling points form a spherical $(2J+S)$-design. We call the associated configurations spin-coherent quantum designs. We further give a fully explicit positive-weight Gauss-Legendre construction that avoids the need for an equal-weight spherical design. Together, these results establish a unified framework for reading out physical observables from a handful of measurement samples, playing for spin systems the role that the so-called von Neumann lattice plays for canonical coherent states.
